title: Apostrophe Ambush
intro: its or it's, whose or who's, plural or possessive — the tiny mark that gives away a rushed writer.

A2.why: “It's” is short for “it is”: it is Monday.
“That's” = “that is”; the apostrophe stands where the “i” was dropped.
“She's” = “she is”; the apostrophe replaces the missing “i”.
“Don't” = “do not”: the apostrophe takes the place of the missing “o”.
The car belongs to Tom, so add 's to his name.
“We're” = “we are”. Without the apostrophe, “were” is the past of “be”.
“It's raining” = “it is raining”. “Its” with no apostrophe means “su”.
“Can't” = “cannot”; the apostrophe sits where letters were removed, between n and t.
One sheriff owns the horse: sheriff + 's.
“I'm” = “I am”: one apostrophe where the “a” was dropped.
“Isn't” = “is not”: the apostrophe replaces the “o”, between n and t.

options: The dog's bone is under the sofa.
The dogs bone is under the sofa.
The dog's' bone is under the sofa.
B1.why: One dog owns the bone: dog + 's.
“Children” is already plural, so it simply takes 's.
“Whose” asks who owns something. “Who's” means “who is” or “who has”.
Here “it's” = “it has”: it has been a long day.
A plural ending in -s just adds the apostrophe after the s: students'.
The house belongs to both parents: plural parents + apostrophe after the s.
“You're” = “you are”. “Your” means “tu” or “vuestro”, as in “your car”.
The name is James, so the 's goes after the whole name (James' is also seen).

options: Who's coming to the Fallas with us?
Whose coming to the Fallas with us?
Whos coming to the Fallas with us?
The cowboys rode into town at dawn.
The cowboy's rode into town at dawn.
The cowboys' rode into town at dawn.
B1.why: Just a plural: more than one cowboy, nothing owned, so no apostrophe.

options: Their paella is the best in the village.
They're paella is the best in the village.
There paella is the best in the village.
B1.why: “Their” shows possession: the paella belongs to them.

B2.why: One company owns the profits: company + 's.

options: It's clear that its meaning changed.
Its clear that it's meaning changed.
It's clear that its' meaning changed.
B2.why: “It's clear” = “it is clear”; “its meaning” is possessive, with no apostrophe.

options: The 1990s were a decade of change.
The 1990's were a decade of change.
The 1990s' were a decade of change.
B2.why: Decades are simple plurals: 1990s, with no apostrophe.

options: Whose idea was it to leave early?
Who's idea was it to leave early?
Whos idea was it to leave early?
B2.why: “Whose” asks about ownership: whose idea? “Who's” would mean “who is”.
One boss: add 's even after a final s, so boss's.
Time phrases can be possessive: two weeks' notice, apostrophe after the plural s.
One team owns the morale: team + 's.

options: There' is no doubt about it.
John Snow's map of cholera deaths changed medicine.
John Snows map of cholera deaths changed medicine.
John Snows' map of cholera deaths changed medicine.
B2.why: The map belongs to John Snow: name + 's.

options: The outlaws' hideout was in the canyon.
The outlaw's hideout was in the canyon.
The outlaws hideout was in the canyon.
B2.why: Several outlaws share the hideout: plural outlaws + apostrophe after the s.

options: The town council has changed its mind.
The town council has changed it's mind.
The town council has changed its' mind.
B2.why: “Its” is possessive, like “his”, with no apostrophe. “It's” always means “it is” or “it has”.

C1.why: Several witnesses: plural witnesses + apostrophe after the s.

options: It's often its own worst enemy.
Its often it's own worst enemy.
Its often its' own worst enemy.
C1.why: “It's often” = “it is often”; “its own” is possessive, with no apostrophe.

options: A day's work deserves a day's pay.
A days work deserves a days pay.
A day's work deserves a days' pay.
C1.why: One day each time: a day's work, a day's pay.
A fixed phrase: “for goodness' sake” keeps just the apostrophe, no extra s.
The Jones family are “the Joneses”, so their garden is “the Joneses'”.

options: He questioned its validity, not theirs.
He questioned it's validity, not their's.
He questioned its' validity, not theirs'.
C1.why: Possessive pronouns (its, theirs, yours, hers) never take an apostrophe.

options: A moment's thought would have helped.
A moments thought would have helped.
A moments' thought would have helped.
C1.why: One moment of thought: a moment's thought, like “a day's work”.

options: Hers was the best paella in the competition.
Her's was the best paella in the competition.
Hers' was the best paella in the competition.
C1.why: “Hers” is a possessive pronoun, like “its” and “theirs”: never an apostrophe.

C1.q: Which is correct? (the people of Valencia)
options: The Valencians' love of fireworks is famous.
The Valencian's love of fireworks is famous.
The Valencians's love of fireworks is famous.
C1.why: Plural Valencians + apostrophe after the s; never add a second s.

options: My sister-in-law's house is in Xàtiva.
My sister's-in-law house is in Xàtiva.
My sister-in-laws house is in Xàtiva.
C1.why: With compound nouns the 's goes at the very end: sister-in-law's.
